contexts.japanesePS3: まぁ、贅沢は言えねぇですな」
contexts.WH: "I just asked the captain, and it sounds like it'll take a full two hours more.  Well, you can't call this luxury."

MG.japanese: 「さっき船長に聞いたら、あと２時間はたっぷり掛かるそうです。まぁ、贅沢は言えねぇですな」
MG.translation: "I just asked the captain, and it sounds like it'll take a full two hours more. Well, beggars can't be choosers."

UP.japanese: 「さっき船長に聞いたら、あと２時間はたっぷり掛かるそうです。まぁ、贅沢は言えねぇですな」
UP.translation: "I just asked the captain, and it sounds like it'll take a full two hours more. Well, beggars can't be choosers."

findings.sourceReading: Amakusa says the crossing takes another full two hours, but they cannot ask for too much or be choosy.
findings.alternative: The boat is plainly inconvenient, and luxury can connect to the literal 贅沢. However the idiom concerns what one can demand under the circumstances rather than whether the trip qualifies as luxurious.

findings.description: あの時の幻を信じたいがために becomes “because it was hard to believe that those events were an illusion,” replacing a wish to believe with difficulty accepting a contrary interpretation.

contexts.japanese: だから、あの時の幻を信じたいがために、旅を続けている。
contexts.japanesePC: だから、あの時の幻を信じたいがために、旅を続けている。
contexts.japanesePS3: だから、あの時の幻を信じたいがために、旅を続けている。
contexts.WH: So, because it was hard to believe that those events were an illusion, I've continued on my journey.
contexts.MG: So, because it was hard to believe that those events were an illusion, I've continued on my journey.
contexts.UP: So, I'm continuing this journey because I want to believe in that illusion.
contexts.note: Parent checked full boat conversation and attributed reflection; canonical contrast independently verified.

MG.japanese:
だから、あの時の幻を信じたいがために、旅を続けている。この旅で何かを変えられるなんて、本気で信じちゃいない。
……いつ旅を終わりにするかも自由。どこを終着点とするかも、自由なのだ。結局、この旅は、私の自己満足のためでしかない……。
MG.translation: So, because it was hard to believe that those events were an illusion, I've continued on my journey. I don't seriously believe that this journey will change anything. ...It's even up to me when to end this journey. It's up to me to choose where the final destination is. In the end, this journey is only for my self-satisfaction...

UP.japanese:
だから、あの時の幻を信じたいがために、旅を続けている。この旅で何かを変えられるなんて、本気で信じちゃいない。
……いつ旅を終わりにするかも自由。どこを終着点とするかも、自由なのだ。結局、この旅は、私の自己満足のためでしかない……。
UP.translation:
So, I'm continuing this journey because I want to believe in that illusion. I don't seriously believe that this journey will change anything.
......I'm even free to end it at any time. It's up to me to choose where the final destination is. In the end, this journey is only for my personal self‐satisfaction......

findings.sourceReading: Ange continues because she wants to believe the vision of that time, despite her doubt and lack of serious expectation that the journey changes anything.
findings.alternative: The preceding paragraph says stopping would mean acknowledging the witch’s message as illusion, so resistance to that acknowledgement is a plausible inference. But the English removes her explicit desire to believe and renders the motive as disbelief in the illusion explanation.

findings.sourceReading: Amakusa says self-satisfaction is perfectly fine, then explains that praise matters only if one can accept it and one need not receive praise to be content.
findings.alternative: His subsequent argument strongly supports self-acceptance, so the overall position remains. The opening statement nevertheless becomes tentative/conditional in frequency where the source is emphatic.

contexts.japanesePS3: ……だとしたら、無欲が一番、人生にやさしいことになるわ。
contexts.WH: "I wonder if humans live so that they can be satisfied.  ......If so, unselfishly is probably the easiest way to live.
contexts.MG: ...If so, it's probably easiest to live without desires.
contexts.UP: ......If so, to seek nothing is probably the easiest way to live.
contexts.note: Complete parent three-witness review restores absence of desire121 and completed journey205206.

MG.japanese: 「ニンゲンってのは、満たされるために生きてるのかしら。……だとしたら、無欲が一番、人生にやさしいことになるわ。…なるほど、七つの大罪のひとつが強欲になるのも納得ね」
MG.translation: "I wonder if Humans live for the purpose of becoming satisfied. ...If so, it's probably easiest to live without desires. ...I see, so that's why greed is one of the seven deadly sins."

UP.japanese: 「ニンゲンってのは、満たされるために生きてるのかしら。……だとしたら、無欲が一番、人生にやさしいことになるわ。…なるほど、七つの大罪のひとつが強欲になるのも納得ね」
UP.translation: "I wonder if Humanhumans live so that they can be satisfied. ......If so, to seek nothing is probably the easiest way to live. ...Yes, it makes sense why greed is one of the seven deadly sins."

findings.sourceReading: If humans live to be fulfilled, having no desires would make life easiest: no remaining wants would need fulfillment.
findings.alternative: 無欲 can carry an unselfish connotation, and Mammon’s greed context makes selfishness relevant. Here the immediately preceding reasoning defines desire as wanting what one lacks, so lack of desire rather than altruism supplies the stated inference.

contexts.MG:
What I'm trying to say...is that the only one who can acknowledge you in this world is you yourself."
Amakusa continued stretching as he spoke.
In an irritatingly fresh way.
Hearing it told to me as though from a teacher made me instinctively want to resist, but what he was saying was extremely sensible.
".........
...That may be true.
People work hard when they want to be acknowledged by someone.
...In most cases, that someone is their parents.
Children learn how to work hard because they want to be praised by their parents.
......Although that's why I never learned."
"Sorry, that's not how I meant it.
...What I'm trying to say is that there's nothing wrong with self-satisfaction.
No matter who praises you, it's meaningless unless you can accept it.
...Turning it around, even if no one praises you, that doesn't matter as long as you can accept it."
"......Self-satisfaction tends to contradict a desire to improve oneself, so we're usually taught that it's bad.
Somehow, your argument seems like a pretty fresh take on it, Amakusa."
"The anguish of the human world comes when you want someone to acknowledge you, but you don't know what it is you should be striving for.
contexts.UP:
What I'm trying to say is that there's no self about it—in this world, the only one capable of satisfying you is yourself."
Amakusa continued stretching as he spoke.
In an annoyingly eloquent way.
Hearing it told to me as though from a teacher made me instinctively want to resist, but what he was saying was extremely sensible.
".....................
......That may be true."
"People work hard when they want to satisfy someone.
......In most cases, that someone is their parents.
Children learn how to work hard because they want to be praised by their parents.
.........Of course, that's why I never learned."
"Sorry, that's not what I intended to say."
"......What I want to say is that self‐satisfaction is {nobr:A‐OK.
No matter who praises you, it's meaningless unless you yourself are satisfied.
......Turning it around, even if no one praises you, that doesn't matter as long as you're satisfied yourself."
".........Self‐satisfaction and self‐improvement contradict each other, so we're usually taught that the former is bad.
Your argument is kind of a breath of fresh air."
"The anguish of the human world comes when you want to satisfy someone, you want recognition, but you don't know where to put the effort.

UP.japanese:
「茶化さんでください。俺が言いたいのは、自己も何も、自分を認められるのは世の中で自分だけしかいないってことです」
「人は、誰かに認められたくて努力をするわ。……多くの場合、それは親ね。親に褒められたくて、子どもは努力を覚える。………だから私は、覚えなかったわけだけど」
「誰かに認めて欲しくて、だけれど何を努力すればいいのかわからないのが、人の世の苦しみです。俺にもそういう頃があった」
UP.translation:
"Don't just laugh it off. What I'm trying to say is that there's no self about it—in this world, the only one capable of satisfying you is yourself."
"People work hard when they want to satisfy someone. ......In most cases, that someone is their parents. Children learn how to work hard because they want to be praised by their parents. .........Of course, that's why I never learned."
"The anguish of the human world comes when you want to satisfy someone, you want recognition, but you don't know where to put the effort. I had a time like that too."

findings.description: MG writes shouldve be possible rather than should be or should have been possible.

contexts.japanese: ……つまり、さくたろうの依り代であるライオンのぬいぐるみが存在しなくても、召喚は可能のはず。
contexts.japanesePS3: ……つまり、さくたろうの依り代であるライオンのぬいぐるみが存在しなくても、召喚は可能のはず。

contexts.UP: ......In other words, even if the stuffed animal lion that was Sakutarou's vessel didn't exist, it should have been possible to summon him.

MG.japanese: 真里亞お姉ちゃんは、さくたろうは死んでしまったと思い、絶望した。それはつまり、もうこうして召喚できなかったという意味だ。召喚には依り代がある方が有利だと、かつてお姉ちゃんは言っていた。しかし、依り代は補助輪のようなもので、絶対必要なものではないはず。……つまり、さくたろうの依り代であるライオンのぬいぐるみが存在しなくても、召喚は可能のはず。
MG.translation: Maria onee-chan had despaired, thinking that Sakutarou had died. Which meant she hadn't been able to summon him like this anymore. In the past, Onee-chan said it was more advantageous in a summoning to have a vessel. However, a vessel is like training wheels, and it shouldn't be absolutely necessary. ...In other words, even if the stuffed animal lion that was Sakutarou's vessel didn't exist, it should've be possible to summon him.
